Our study identifies a robust exosomal miRNA signature for PD classification and reveals the convergence of mitochondrial dysfunction and peripheral immune dysregulation as core pathological features, establishing a foundation for exosome-based liquid biopsy and mechanistic biomarker development.

title: Nigrosome-1 neuromelanin and iron coupling in idiopathic and GBA-associated Parkinson disease
authors: the Catalonian Neuroimaging Parkinson’s disease Consortium
abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) involves early neuromelanin (NM) loss, iron dysregulation and often shows asymmetric motor onset. We quantified NM- and iron-sensitive MRI measures in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and nigrosome-1 (N1) in idiopathic PD (iPD, n = 30), GBA -associated PD (GBA-PD, n = 26) and in healthy controls (HC, n = 30), by performing magnitude-based metrics, asymmetry indices and cross-modal coupling analyses. Both PD groups showed reduced NM-sensitive and increased iron-sensitive signal relative to HC, with the strongest alterations in N1. NM-sensitive N1 markers provided the best patient-control discrimination, particularly between GBA-PD and HC (AUCLOOCV = 0.91). N1 NM asymmetry and most robustly N1 NM contrast ratio (CR), moderately distinguished HC from patient subgroups (AUCLOOCV range = 0.71-0.72). Asymmetry index (AI) metrics did not differentiate iPD from GBA-PD. The NM-iron coupling pattern observed in HC was inverted in PD. Exploratory analyses suggested a GBA1 severity-related variation in N1 NM-iron coupling. These findings identify N1 as the main subregion where multimodal MRI captures the PD-related nigral degeneration.

title: Longitudinal blood-based proteomics reveal progression-specific molecular signatures in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) shows marked heterogeneity in clinical progression and single baseline biomarkers have shown limited value for predicting these changes. We examined whether repeated serum proteomics can identify protein-clinical associations linked to worsening across motor, cognitive, non-motor, and treatment-related outcomes. We analysed 166 patients with PD from the prospective PROMOVE registry with repeated OFF-state clinical assessments and longitudinal serum proteomics covering 297 proteins. For each outcome, participants were classified as worsening or non-worsening based on individual longitudinal slopes. In worsening participants, all proteins were tested using linear mixed-effects models that separated within- from between-subject protein effects. Six associations remained significant after FDR correction. Higher DDC was associated with increasing levodopa equivalent daily dose. Higher CD276 and POSTN were associated with worse MDS-UPDRS II scores, while higher VEGF-C and IL19 were associated with worse MDS-UPDRS III scores. Higher IL12 was associated with lower MMSE scores. The five non-treatment associations remained significant after additional adjustment for time-varying dopaminergic treatment. Repeated serum proteomics identified distinct protein-clinical associations in patients showing clinical worsening. The findings point to treatment-related, immune, vascular, and extracellular-matrix processes and suggest that longitudinal proteomics may complement clinical measures when monitoring PD progression.

title: Parkinson’s disease progression and fronto-temporal disconnection relate to identity of minor hallucinations
abstract: Presence hallucinations (PH), a non-veridical perceptions of someone appearing around you, are frequent symptoms in Parkinson’s disease (PD). They belong to the group of minor hallucinations, predicting later appearance of structured visual hallucinations and PD psychosis. Despite their elevated frequency and negative clinical outcomes, differences in PH subtypes have not been examined. Investigating PD patients with identified versus unidentified PH, this study aims to determine differences in disease progression, motor and cognitive performance, and brain mechanisms. From 77 PD patients, 27 reporting PH were grouped into those with identified PH versus unidentified PH (iPH-PD, n = 12; uPH-PD, n = 15). Disease progression (UPDRS, Hoehn Yahr), cognitive functions (PD-CRS) (with exploratory analysis of all clinical variables, uncorrected for multiple comparisons), sensitivity to robot-induced PH and resting-state functional connectivity were analysed. iPH reports mostly consisted of first-degree close others (e.g., partner). iPH-PD patients had a more advanced PD stage, reported more daily-life motor impairments and simple visual illusions than uPH-PD patients. Both groups showed similar sensitivity to robot-induced PH. Resting-state functional connectivity showed that iPH-PD vs. uPH-PD patients had right IFG-pMTG functional disconnection within a previously defined PH network and the degree of this disconnection correlated with posterior cognitive impairment. Distinguishing iPH-PD from uPH-PD patients, we show that the former display worse daily motor functioning, more frequent visual illusions and stronger fronto-temporal disconnection, related to cognitive dysfunction. Although the present findings need to be confirmed in larger samples, they suggest that iPH-PD have a more advanced form of PD, possibly representing an intermediate disease stage, between uPH-PD and PD patients with structured visual hallucinations.

title: Association of diffusion along the perivascular spaces with clinical symptoms and dopaminergic degeneration in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between the diffusion tensor image (DTI) analysis along the perivascular space (ALPS) index, striatal dopamine transporter (DAT) availability, and baseline motor and cognitive function in 207 patients with newly diagnosed Parkinson’s disease (PD). All patients underwent brain MRI and 18 F-FP-CIT PET scans, and ALPS index was calculated to assess glymphatic system function. Multiple linear regression analyses demonstrated that ALPS index and DAT availability in the posterior putamen were negatively associated with the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale Part III (UPDRS-III) scores. Mediation analyses showed that ALPS index affected UPDRS-III scores both directly ( β = −10.116, P = 0.002) and indirectly via DAT availability in the posterior putamen ( β = 2.509, P = 0.036). Furthermore, ALPS index and DAT availability in the associative striatum were positively associated with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores. The ALPS index affected MMSE scores both directly ( β = 1.317, P = 0.003) and indirectly via DAT availability in the anterior putamen ( β = −0.169, P = 0.047). The relationship between ALPS index and baseline motor or cognitive function was significant only when striatal dopamine was severely depleted. These findings suggest that glymphatic dysfunction is associated with worse motor and cognitive function in PD and may exert stronger effects when striatal dopamine is severely depleted.

title: Distinct subthalamic and pallidal beta dynamics in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Despite the clinical use as a Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) target in Parkinson’s disease (PD) and recent approval for adaptive stimulation, beta dynamics in the Globus Pallidus internus (GPi) remain poorly defined compared to the Subthalamic Nucleus (STN). We investigated target-specific beta activity in Local Field Potentials recorded in PD patients implanted with sensing-enabled STN- or GPi-DBS and examined differential modulation by L-Dopa and stimulation and relationship with motor symptoms. In the untreated state, spectral profiles were comparable between targets. L-Dopa selectively reduced low-beta power and burst durations in the STN, while suppressing high-beta activity in the GPi. DBS induced broadband beta suppression and burst shortening in the STN, whereas attenuated pallidal high-beta oscillations. Clinical improvement correlated with low-beta modulation in STN patients and high-beta modulation in GPi patients. Low- and high-beta sub-bands exhibit distinct target-specific pathophysiological behaviour and responsiveness. These findings provide a physiological framework for frequency-tailored adaptive DBS.

title: Beyond dopamine: the role of non-dopaminergic systems in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) has long been considered a disorder of dopamine depletion. However, dopaminergic dysfunction alone cannot explain its clinical complexity. Emerging evidence implicates non-dopaminergic systems degeneration/dysregulation‌ as critical contributors to PD’s multifaceted pathology. Integrating these systems into a framework of network dysfunction, this review synthesizes current knowledge on the role of non-dopaminergic systems in PD pathogenesis, symptomatology, and therapeutic advancement, advocating for a paradigm shift toward multisystem-targeted therapies.

title: An exploratory remote pilot study of environmental risk factors for Lewy body dementia considering sex differences
abstract: Lewy body dementia (LBD), including Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), is a common dementia that currently lacks disease modification. While studies in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases underscore the contribution of environmental factors with sex differences, knowledge on LBD environmental risk factors remains limited. We conducted an exploratory remote pilot survey, including data on residential history, chemical exposure, smoking, and alcohol use, for people with LBD ( n = 130; 51 females, 79 males) and age-matched controls ( n = 124; 64 females, 60 males). Associations with LBD risk for each environmental factor were assessed in the overall cohort and stratified by sex and LBD subtype (DLB or PDD). Metal exposure was associated with a higher risk of LBD. Alcohol and smoking were associated with a higher risk, particularly for males; glue/adhesives and not living in the suburbs were associated with a higher risk, particularly for females. Environmental factors likely play a role in LBD with potential sex differences.

title: The brain lymphatic drainage system: structure, physiological functions, and pathological involvement in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: The brain lymphatic drainage system, a synergistic clearance axis consisting of the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels, breaks the previous dogma that the lymphatic system is absent in the brain. The brain lymphatic drainage system has multiple physiological functions and is found to be related to Parkinson’s disease (PD) in both animal and human studies. α-synuclein (α-syn) protein, when misfolded, along with its post-translational modified forms plays a crucial role in PD, leading to the formation of cytotoxic oligomers and aggregates that result in neurodegeneration. There are reports showing that dysfunction of the brain lymphatic drainage system is associated with accumulation of α-syn and may be involved in neuroinflammation, immune disorder, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which are also pathogenic mechanisms of PD. However, the exact role of the brain lymphatic drainage system in PD pathogenesis remains unclear. This review systematically summarizes the structure of the brain lymphatic drainage system, its physiological functions, and pathological involvement in PD, and illustrates clinical imaging findings of PD. Finally, this review discusses the future directions that may help intervene in the brain lymphatic drainage system during the pathogenesis of PD.

title: Brain-first body-first model translated to individual-level characterization in Parkinson’s disease: multimodal imaging and clinical approach
abstract: The brain-first/body-first hypothesis of Parkinson’s disease (PD) proposes two distinct trajectories of disease initiation and propagation. Body-first PD involves early peripheral (autonomic) pathology, including abnormal cardiac sympathetic imaging and brainstem-related REM-sleep behavior disorder (RBD), whereas brain-first PD is thought to originate centrally before spreading peripherally. Substantial criticism has recently been raised about this dichotomous model, largely derived from group-level data and its applicability to individual patients remains unclear. We examined to what degree commonly used, clinical and imaging features can assist in classifying individual early PD patients (≤2 years since diagnosis, n = 20) into brain-first and body-first subtypes, using 123 I-MIBG scintigraphy as the reference standard. Probable RBD status was the strongest individual-level classification marker, correctly classifying 85% of patients. Other clinical and imaging features performed poor as individual-level classifiers, suggesting substantial overlap, a continuum, and limited individual-level differentiation. RBD is associated with MIBG-defined body-first PD in this cohort, and may represent a promising, low-cost marker needing further validation.

title: Mapping symptom domains and laterality to substantia nigra subregions in early Parkinson’s disease using neuromelanin MRI
abstract: Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) visualizes the substantia nigra (SN) and aids the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease (PD), but whether its subregions map onto specific symptoms is unclear. In 105 patients with early PD, the SN was parcellated into ventral (associative), medial (limbic) and dorsolateral (sensorimotor) subregions. Compared with 50 reference participants, volumes were reduced bilaterally in all subregions (all p < 0.001); within patients, the loss was greater on the more affected side in the ventral, dorsolateral and total SN and symmetric in the medial SN. Volumes were correlated with the OFF-state MDS-UPDRS Part III, the MMSE, the cardiovagal and adrenergic subscores of the Composite Autonomic Scoring Scale (CASS) and orthostatic hypotension (OH). When each SN side was matched to its contralateral-body score, dorsolateral volume was the strongest correlate of motor severity (all FDR q ≤ 0.012). For symptoms without a lateralized counterpart, the correlations were carried by the less affected side ( q < 0.05): dorsolateral volume with the axial subscore ( r = −0.287) and OH ( r = −0.289), and medial volume with the cardiovagal ( r = −0.355) and adrenergic ( r = −0.336) subscores. In early PD, subregional NM-MRI volumes show symptom-oriented, laterality-dependent associations, with the dorsolateral SN tracking lateralized motor severity and the less affected medial SN relating to cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction.

title: Precision prediction of motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson’s disease via multiregional neural sensing
abstract: Precise prediction of motor fluctuations is critical for the management of advanced Parkinson’s disease (PD). However, current single-region biomarkers show poor performance largely due to their mismatch with the network-level pathophysiology. This study presents a translatable multi-regional sensing framework for simultaneous recording from eight cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (CBGT) circuit hubs in rodent models. Application of a hierarchical loss-optimized multilayer perceptron (H-Lo-MLP) tailored for open-set clinical scenarios demonstrates that distributed CBGT oscillatory patterns substantially outperform single-region biomarkers. The H-Lo-MLP achieves nearly 90% prediction accuracy, far exceeding the ~50% of threshold-based approaches, with robust generalizability across disease progression and dopaminergic modulation. Systematic evaluation of all 255 region combinations identifies primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal striatum as pivotal discriminative hubs and reveals a parsimonious four-region configuration that retains near-optimal predictive performance while minimizing surgical invasiveness. Cross-species proof-of-concept in a single non-human primate recapitulates the conserved centrality of M1 and demonstrates the feasibility of simultaneous multi-region monitoring via a single linear electrode. These findings establish network-level sensing as a clinically viable paradigm for precise motor fluctuation prediction, overcoming limitations of constrained adaptive deep brain stimulation. By validating a surgically tractable, cross-species network-sensing approach, this work bridges the gap between circuit-level pathophysiology and clinical translation.

title: Maternal immune activation primes adult offspring for insult-dependent Parkinsonian vulnerability in male mice
abstract: Maternal immune activation (MIA) can persistently alter offspring neuroimmune functions, but its contribution to the susceptibility to neurodegenerative diseases remains unclear. We tested whether Poly(I:C)-induced MIA enhances a latent vulnerability to mechanistically distinct PD-related insults. Single-cell RNA sequencing of adult offspring's brain revealed broadly preserved cellular composition but identified a disease-relevant transcriptional signature centered on astrocytes. Astrocytic differentially expressed genes were enriched for Parkinson's disease and broader neurodegenerative pathways, suggesting that MIA programs an adult astrocyte-linked susceptibility state. Consistent with this indication, MIA offspring challenged with MPTP developed exacerbated motor deficits, greater loss of dopaminergic neurons in the nigrostriatal system, and enhanced GFAP+ astrocyte reactivity. MIA offspring challenged with α-synuclein preformed fibrils (PFF) also showed worsened motor dysfunction and dopaminergic injury, but without a detectable increase in GFAP+ astrocyte density. Thus, MIA establishes a latent vulnerability that is revealed by later PD-related injury rather than directly causing adult Parkinsonism. The expression of this vulnerability is insult-dependent. These findings identify developmental immune programming as a modifier of adult nigrostriatal resilience and implicate astrocyte-linked molecular states as a disease primer between early-life inflammation and later neurodegenerative risk.

title: Bridge funding through a non-profit partnership to sustain disrupted neurodegenerative research and early career investigators
abstract: In response to recent United States federal funding changes, the Alzheimer’s Association and The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, with philanthropic partners, created the Bridge Funding for Disrupted Neurodegenerative research program. Eighteen projects spanning disease risk mechanisms, prevention, basic biology, biomarkers, and population studies were funded, sustaining research momentum and early career scientists during funding uncertainty. Continued federal and non-profit investment is needed to sustain this progress.

title: Oculomotor and clinical correlates with impaired optokinetic nystagmus in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Abnormalities in eye movement are promising indicators of Parkinson’s disease (PD); however, the role of optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) in PD remains poorly understood. In this study, we addressed this gap by investigating the performance of OKN in individuals with PD and its correlation with other ocular and clinical characteristics. A cohort comprising 251 patients with PD and 46 age-matched healthy controls (HCs) underwent comprehensive oculomotor assessments. These assessments included the recording of OKN, visually guided saccades, and smooth pursuit eye movements (SPEM) across three motion frequencies along the horizontal axis. Patients with PD were clinically evaluated using a series of scales for both motor and non-motor symptoms. The associations between key oculomotor parameters and clinical phenotypes in patients with PD were investigated. Compared to HCs, patients with PD presented significantly reduced OKN gain. The OKN gain was strongly correlated with saccade latency and SPEM gain across all tested frequencies but not with saccade accuracy. Among all eye movement parameters, OKN gain and saccade latency were associated primarily with the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (FOG-Q) score and cognitive score. After controlling for confounding variables, however, OKN gain, rather than saccade latency, was independently associated with the occurrence of FOG in patients with PD. Next, we developed a predictive model, incorporating factors such as age, OKN gain, scores from the MDS-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale Part III (MDS-UPDRS-III), the Chinese version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment-Basic (MoCA-BC), and the presence of the wearing-off phenomenon. This model had an accuracy rate of 80.4% in predicting the risk of FOG. We found that OKN is impaired and associated with saccade and SPEM performance in PD patients. Reduced optokinetic gain may increase the likelihood of the FOG phenotype in PD patients.
